seoDescription: Hurt on a motorcycle in Dearborn Heights? Under Michigan no-fault a motorcycle is not a “motor vehicle,” which decides who pays your medical bills. This page covers the rider priority rule, U-turns across Telegraph’s median crossovers and Ford Road’s left turns and driveways, parked cars and car doors on Warren, Hines Drive, single-vehicle crashes with no PIP claim, which agency owns the road, the helmet law, and the deadlines. Free review. (313) 406-7606.

c.v: The recurring account in rider cases is a driver turning left across oncoming traffic who misjudges the speed of a motorcycle or never sees it. Under Michigan law, a driver must yield to oncoming traffic before turning left (MCL 257.650). On Telegraph, left turns are made as U-turns at the median crossovers, where the turning driver crosses four lanes, and a motorcycle in the far lane is easy to miss behind a car or truck in the nearer one. sections.heading: Who pays a Dearborn Heights rider’s medical bills

c.v: If a car or truck was involved, you have no-fault benefits, but not from your motorcycle insurer.
Under MCL 500.3114(5), your Personal Injury Protection benefits come, in order, from:

items.v: the insurer of the owner or registrant of the motor vehicle involved
the insurer of that vehicle’s operator
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s operator
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s owner or registrant

c.v: Priority follows the vehicles’ insurers, not who was at fault. “Involved” does not require contact; a car that cut you off is involved even if it never touched you. If no insurer in that chain exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan pays (MCL 500.3172), with its $250,000 medical cap, unless you owned the motorcycle and it was uninsured (MCL 500.3113(b)). In a crash with an uninsured driver, and with no car policy of your own in the household, the Assigned Claims Plan is often where the claim goes.
The benefits are the ones a driver would get under MCL 500.3107:

items.v: medical expenses, up to the PIP limit on the policy that pays
85 percent of lost wages for up to three years, up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each year
$20 a day in replacement services
attendant care
mileage

c.v: Written notice is due within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). See our

The first medical limit is set by a policy you did not choose. Since the 2019 reform, the PIP medical level on the policy first in priority pays first; if the driver who hit you chose $250,000, or a lower level, that policy pays up to its limit, and a lower-priority policy with more coverage, such as your own car policy, may then pay the rest. This is why optional first-party medical coverage on a motorcycle policy matters.
If no car or truck was involved, no-fault does not apply.
Several common crashes produce no PIP claim:

items.v: a slide on flood sand or leaves on Hines Drive
a deer strike in the park with no other vehicle involved
a pothole or broken pavement seam on a county road or City street
a low-speed drop in a parking lot

c.v: Your bills go to your health insurance and to any medical coverage you bought on the motorcycle policy. Any injury claim is against whoever caused the hazard, if anyone did. A car that forced you to swerve is a vehicle “involved” in the crash, and that changes the answer. A car door opened into your path may be too, depending on the parked-vehicle rules (MCL 500.3106).
Your own collision or comprehensive coverage pays for the bike. The mini tort claim does not cover a motorcycle, because a motorcycle is not a “motor vehicle” under the no-fault act (

sections.heading: Your claim against the driver who hit you

c.v: For pain and suffering and economic losses beyond no-fault, you can sue the at-fault driver if your injury meets the threshold: serious impairment of body function, permanent serious disfigurement, or death (MCL 500.3135). A serious impairment is an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects your general ability to lead your normal life. It does not have to be permanent (
Motorcycle injuries often clear that threshold. Common examples include:

items.v: fractures
road rash requiring grafts
torn ligaments

c.v: You also recover excess economic damages above the PIP limit that applied to you, including lost wages above the monthly cap (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)). You have three years to sue (MCL 600.5805(2)). A fatal crash is brought by the estate through the Wayne County Probate Court. The wrongful death claim also has three years, with an extension for the estate’s personal representative (MCL 600.5852). See our

c.v: Since 2012, Michigan has let riders 21 and older ride without a helmet if they meet two conditions (MCL 257.658):

items.v: They carry at least $20,000 in first-party medical coverage.
They have either held a motorcycle endorsement for two years or passed an approved safety course.

c.v: Riders under 21 must wear a helmet, and a passenger has rules of their own. If you met those conditions, riding without a helmet was legal, so it was not a traffic violation. In a head-injury case, the insurer will argue a helmet would have reduced the injury. That is a damages and causation argument for the jury, not a bar to the claim. In a leg or shoulder case, it is irrelevant.

faqs.question: A driver made a U-turn across Telegraph in front of me. Who is at fault?

answer.v: Usually the turning driver, who must yield to oncoming traffic, including a motorcycle. At a Telegraph crossover the turning driver crosses four lanes, and insurers will argue your speed or lane position. Store cameras and witnesses matter, and footage is overwritten within days.

faqs.question: A parked driver opened a door into me on Warren Avenue. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Usually. A driver must not open a door into traffic unless it is safe to do so, and the parked car is a vehicle involved in the crash. Whether no-fault covers your medical bills in that situation is a technical question under the parked-vehicle rules, so the facts of how the door was opened matter. Get the driver’s name, plate, and insurance, and photograph the car and the door.

faqs.question: A car crossed the center line on a Hines Drive curve and I went off the road. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Usually. The car is “involved” under no-fault whether or not it touched you, so its owner’s insurer is first in line for your medical bills. Your claim for pain and suffering is against the driver. Get the plate and witnesses, because the car may not stop.

faqs.question: Does the at-fault driver’s insurance pay my medical bills?

answer.v: Not because the driver was at fault. Under the rider priority rule, the insurer of the car involved pays first, whoever caused the crash. Fault matters for your separate claim for pain and suffering.

faqs.question: The driver who hit me had no insurance. Who pays my medical bills?

answer.v: If the car was uninsured, the next insurer in the priority chain pays: the driver’s own insurer, if the driver insures another vehicle; then your own car insurer; then the car insurer of the motorcycle’s owner. If there is none, the Assigned Claims Plan pays, up to $250,000 in medical benefits. Your pain-and-suffering claim depends on uninsured motorist coverage on your motorcycle policy.

faqs.question: I have my own car insurance. Doesn’t that cover me on the motorcycle?

answer.v: Not first. If a car was involved, that car’s insurer is first in line. Your own car insurer is third, after the involved vehicle’s owner’s and operator’s insurers. A motorcycle policy itself does not carry Michigan PIP. If no car was involved, there is usually no PIP claim at all.

faqs.question: I wasn’t wearing a helmet. Can I still recover?

answer.v: Yes, if three conditions were met: - you were 21 or older - you carried the required $20,000 in medical coverage - you had either two years of endorsement or a safety course. The insurer can argue a helmet would have reduced a head injury. That goes to damages, not to whether you have a claim.

- One year to notify the responsible no-fault insurer. - Three years to sue the at-fault driver, and three years for a wrongful death claim. - 120 days for a notice to Wayne County or the City. - 120 days for a road-defect notice against MDOT. - 120 days for a dram shop notice, and two years to sue a bar.
